CausalChain: Chronic liver injury/NASH conditions -> Impaired system Xc− activity and cystine uptake -> Glutathione depletion and heightened ROS/lipid peroxidation -> Activation of hepatic transsulfuration pathway from methionine -> Enhanced endogenous cysteine synthesis -> Sustained glutathione production -> Suppression of ferroptosis -> Attenuation of liver damage progression
Hypothesis: Enhancing the hepatic transsulfuration pathway, for example via dietary methionine supplementation or pharmacological activation, can increase endogenous cysteine and glutathione production, thereby reducing ferroptosis and mitigating the progression of non‐alcoholic steatohepatitis.
Abstract: In hepatic diseases, especially non‐alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation are critical drivers of cell death via ferroptosis. While impairment of system Xc− limits cystine uptake and depletes glutathione reserves, hepatocytes may activate the transsulfuration pathway to synthesize cysteine from methionine, thereby sustaining glutathione production and countering ferroptotic damage. We propose that targeted enhancement of the hepatic transsulfuration pathway could fortify antioxidant defenses, reducing lipid peroxidation and mitigating progression from simple steatosis to NASH. This approach suggests a promising therapeutic avenue whereby dietary or pharmacological interventions that boost endogenous cysteine synthesis actively suppress ferroptosis-induced liver injury.
